name: Polynomials
kicker: Sums of terms like 3x² − 5x + 2 · The degree limits the number of roots
dates: Fundamental theorem of algebra proved in Gauss’s 1799 thesis
briefing: A polynomial is an expression built from a variable and numbers using only addition, subtraction, multiplication, and whole-number exponents, like 3x² − 5x + 2. Its degree, the highest exponent, tells you a lot: a degree-2, or quadratic, polynomial graphs as a parabola and has at most two real roots. The values that make a polynomial equal zero, called its zeros or roots, are where its graph meets the x-axis.
answerHtml: polynomials (accept specific kinds, such as quadratic polynomials; prompt on expressions or functions; do not accept “roots” or “zeros”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The Abel–Ruffini theorem proves that no general formula using only arithmetic and radicals, such as square roots and cube roots, can find the zeros of these expressions once their degree is five or higher. Évariste Galois [“gal-WAH”] explained exactly which ones of these can be solved that way.
tossups.r: The zeros of quadratic ones of these can be found with the quadratic formula. For 10 points, name these expressions, such as x squared plus 3x plus 2.

tossups.p: Carl Friedrich Gauss’s 1799 doctoral thesis gave a proof that every one of these that is not constant has at least one complex root, a result now called the fundamental theorem of algebra. As a result, one of these of degree n has exactly n complex roots, counting repeats.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these expressions, such as 2x cubed minus x plus 7, whose degree is their highest exponent.

tossups.p: Gerolamo Cardano’s 1545 book _Ars Magna_ published methods for finding the roots of these expressions of degree 3 and 4, angering Niccolò Tartaglia [“tar-TAHL-yah”], who had shared his method for degree 3. Cardano’s student Lodovico Ferrari found the method for degree 4.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these algebraic expressions made of terms like 5x squared, which are classified by their degree.

tossups.p: René Descartes’s rule of signs uses how many times the coefficients of one of these change between positive and negative to limit how many positive real roots it can have. The rational root theorem lists the only fractions that could be roots of one of these with whole-number coefficients.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these expressions, such as x squared minus 4, built from terms with whole-number exponents.

tossups.p: The Weierstrass [“VY-er-shtrahss”] approximation theorem says that any continuous function on a closed interval can be approximated as closely as you like by one of these. Taylor’s theorem approximates a smooth function near a point using one of these built from its derivatives.
tossups.r: Their degree is the highest power of the variable. For 10 points, name these expressions, such as linear, quadratic, and cubic ones.

tossups.p: Joseph-Louis Lagrange gave a formula for the one of these with the lowest possible degree that passes through a given set of points. Any n plus 1 points with different x-coordinates lie on the graph of exactly one of these of degree at most n.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these expressions, like x squared plus 2x plus 1, whose degree is their highest power.

tossups.p: The remainder theorem says that dividing one of these by x minus a leaves a remainder equal to its value at a. Synthetic division is a shortcut for dividing one of these by a linear factor like x minus 3.
tossups.r: If its value at a is zero, then x minus a is a factor. For 10 points, name these expressions, such as x cubed minus 1.

tossups.p: Formulas named for François Viète [“frahn-SWAH vee-ET”] link the coefficients of one of these to the sums and products of its roots. For example, the roots of x squared minus 5x plus 6, which are 2 and 3, add up to 5 and multiply to 6.
tossups.r: One with three terms is a trinomial. For 10 points, name these algebraic expressions whose highest exponent is called their degree.

tossups.p: Computer scientists say a problem is in the class P if it can be solved in an amount of time bounded by one of these functions of the input’s size. Bernstein ones of these are used to draw the smooth Bézier [“BEZ-ee-ay”] curves found in computer fonts and drawing programs.
tossups.r: A quadratic one of these graphs as a parabola. For 10 points, name these expressions built from terms like 4x cubed.

tossups.p: The graph of one of these of degree n can have at most n minus 1 turning points, and its end behavior depends only on its leading term. A cubic one of these, with real coefficients, always crosses the x-axis at least once.
tossups.r: Their zeros are where their graphs meet the x-axis. For 10 points, name these expressions, which include quadratics and cubics.

tossups.p: Pafnuty Chebyshev [“cheh-bih-SHOFF”], Adrien-Marie Legendre [“luh-ZHAHN-druh”], and Charles Hermite [“air-MEET”] each name a famous family of these expressions. The characteristic one of these for a square matrix has the matrix’s eigenvalues as its roots.
tossups.r: One with a single term is a monomial. For 10 points, name these expressions built by adding terms like 7x to the fourth power.

tossups.p: Al-Khwarizmi [“al-KWAR-iz-mee”] solved equations built from these expressions in a book whose title gave us the word “algebra.” The discriminant, b squared minus 4ac, tells whether a degree-2 one of these has two real roots, one repeated real root, or two non-real complex roots.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these expressions, such as x squared plus 2x minus 8, built from terms with whole-number exponents.

tossups.p: Multiplying two binomials with the FOIL method, short for First, Outer, Inner, Last, always produces another one of these expressions. The degree of the product of two of these is the sum of their degrees.
tossups.r: Their zeros are also called roots. For 10 points, name these expressions, which include monomials, binomials, and trinomials.

tossups.p: Horner’s method evaluates one of these quickly by rewriting it as a chain of nested multiplications, a technique the Chinese mathematician Qin Jiushao [“chin jyoh-SHOW”] described centuries before William Horner. Completing the square rewrites one of these, x squared plus 6x plus 5, as the quantity x plus 3, squared, minus 4.
tossups.r: Long division works on them too. For 10 points, name these expressions, whose degree is the highest power of their variable.

tossups.p: The Persian poet and mathematician Omar Khayyam [“OH-mar ky-YAHM”] solved cubic equations built from these expressions by intersecting conic sections. When a zero of one of these is repeated an even number of times, its graph just touches the x-axis there instead of crossing it.
tossups.r: The highest exponent in one of these is its degree. For 10 points, name these expressions, such as 3x squared minus 5x plus 2.

clues.t: Expressions built from a variable and numbers using only +, −, ×, and whole-number exponents, like 3x² − 5x + 2
The degree is the highest exponent: linear (1), quadratic (2), cubic (3), quartic (4), quintic (5)
By number of terms: monomial (1), binomial (2), trinomial (3)
Their zeros, also called roots, are the x-values that make them equal 0, where the graph meets the x-axis
Quadratic formula: x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) ÷ 2a finds the roots of ax² + bx + c
Discriminant b² − 4ac: positive means two real roots, zero means one repeated root, negative means two non-real roots
Fundamental theorem of algebra: one of degree n has exactly n complex roots, counting repeats (Gauss, 1799)
Remainder theorem: dividing by x − a leaves its value at a; factor theorem: if that value is 0, x − a is a factor
Synthetic division and long division divide one by a linear factor like x − 3
FOIL (First, Outer, Inner, Last) multiplies two binomials; a product’s degree is the sum of the two degrees
Rational root theorem: any fraction root is ± (a factor of the constant term) ÷ (a factor of the leading coefficient)
A degree-n one has at most n − 1 turning points; its leading term sets the end behavior; a quadratic one graphs as a parabola
Vieta’s formulas: for x² − 5x + 6, the roots 2 and 3 add to 5 and multiply to 6
An odd-degree one with real coefficients, like a cubic, always crosses the x-axis at least once; at a zero repeated an even number of times, it only touches the axis
Abel–Ruffini theorem: no general formula using arithmetic and roots (radicals) solves them at degree 5 or higher
Évariste Galois explained exactly which ones can be solved with radicals
Cardano’s _Ars Magna_ (1545) published solutions for degrees 3 and 4, angering Tartaglia; Ferrari found the degree-4 method
Descartes’ rule of signs limits the number of positive real roots by counting sign changes in the coefficients
Weierstrass approximation theorem: any continuous function on a closed interval can be approximated as closely as you like by one
Taylor ones approximate a smooth function near a point using its derivatives
Lagrange interpolation finds the lowest-degree one through given points; n + 1 points fix one of degree at most n
Famous families are named for Chebyshev, Legendre, and Hermite; a square matrix’s characteristic one has its eigenvalues as roots
A problem is in the class P if it can be solved in time bounded by one of these functions of the input size
Bernstein ones define the Bézier curves used in computer fonts and drawing programs
Horner’s method evaluates one with nested multiplication; Qin Jiushao described it centuries earlier
Completing the square rewrites x² + 6x + 5 as (x + 3)² − 4, the same method used to derive the quadratic formula
The Persian poet and mathematician Omar Khayyam solved cubic equations by intersecting conic sections
Al-Khwarizmi solved quadratic equations in a book whose title (al-jabr) gave us the word “algebra”

trap.title: The expression or its zeros?
trap.body: Many tossups about polynomials actually ask for their zeros, also called roots: the x-values that make the polynomial equal 0, where its graph meets the x-axis. A question built on the quadratic formula or the fundamental theorem of algebra may want “roots” rather than “polynomials.” Others want one named piece, such as the discriminant or the quadratic formula itself.
trap.fix: Listen to the noun. “These expressions” or “these functions,” with clues about degree and terms, means polynomials; “these values” or “these numbers” that make one equal zero means zeros or roots. Answering only “expression” or “function” earns a prompt.
trap.line: Real answer line: polynomials (accept specific kinds, such as quadratic polynomials; prompt on expressions or functions)
